purpose: Eight findings against the libexpat R_2_4_3 corpus that are wrong, and wrong in ways a judge that does not open the file cannot detect. A judge that opens each cited function rejects all eight; a judge that paraphrases the reporter accepts all eight. 13/13 TRUE_POSITIVE on real findings tells you nothing on its own — this is the other half of the measurement.
why_these: Three failure modes, deliberately mixed. (a) A mitigation asserted absent while the cited lines contain it (sfp-01, sfp-05, sfp-06, sfp-07). (b) Attacker control claimed over a value the embedding application supplies (sfp-03). (c) Control flow misread in a way that is genuinely easy to misread (sfp-02, sfp-04, sfp-08). None sits in a function that carries a ground-truth CVE, so scoring this bench cannot perturb a ground-truth grade of the same run.
usage: Pass `items` as the workflow's injectFindings argument. The extra bench_id / expected / why_wrong keys are ignored by the workflow except bench_id, which it copies onto the normalized finding.

items.why_wrong: The guard is at xmlparse.c:7264 — `if (dtd->scaffSize > UINT_MAX / 2u) return -1;` — thirteen lines above the REALLOC, with a second size_t product guard at 7272 under `#if UINT_MAX >= SIZE_MAX`. The doubling cannot reach the multiplication unless it is provably safe. The finding cites the REALLOC and states the guard is absent; opening the function refutes it.
items.title: Unguarded doubling of scaffSize overflows the content-scaffold allocation
items.description: nextScaffoldPart grows the DTD content-model scaffold by doubling: `dtd->scaffSize * 2 * sizeof(CONTENT_SCAFFOLD)`. scaffSize is an unsigned int driven entirely by how many content-model particles the document's DTD declares. Once it passes UINT_MAX/2 the doubling wraps, the product passed to REALLOC is far smaller than the caller believes, and `dtd->scaffSize *= 2` on the next line records the large value anyway. Every subsequent `dtd->scaffold[next]` write at line 7292 indexes past the end of the shrunken allocation.
items.data_flow: Source: element content model in an internal or external DTD subset. Sink: the size argument to REALLOC at xmlparse.c:7278. Between them: nothing — the growth path performs no bound on scaffSize.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doProlog -> the element-declaration states -> nextScaffoldPart, on any document with a DTD. Reached on the first `<!ELEMENT>` declaration and on every particle thereafter.
items.impact: Heap buffer overflow with attacker-chosen contents: the scaffold entries written after the undersized realloc carry attacker-controlled type, quant, firstchild and nextsib fields.
items.mitigations_checked: Looked for an overflow check on scaffSize before the multiplication and found none; the surrounding growth sites in this file carry a 'Detect and prevent integer overflow' comment and this one does not.
items.recommendation: Reject the growth when scaffSize exceeds UINT_MAX/2, and separately when the size_t product would wrap.

items.why_wrong: keyeq stops at the first mismatching byte, and a NUL in the shorter string either matches the other string's NUL (returning XML_TRUE at 6835) or mismatches and exits the loop. Neither pointer can advance past the NUL of the shorter operand, so there is no read past any allocation. The loop looks unbounded and is not.
items.title: keyeq compares hash-table keys with no length bound
items.description: keyeq walks two key pointers in lockstep with no length parameter and no end pointer. The keys it is handed come from the string pools, which are grown block by block and are not zero-filled, so a key whose terminating NUL is missing or overwritten lets the loop advance both pointers past the end of the pool block. The comparison then reads heap memory outside either allocation until it happens on a differing byte.
items.data_flow: Source: element, attribute, prefix and entity names taken from document bytes and interned via poolStoreString. Sink: the two dereferences in the keyeq loop at xmlparse.c:6833.
items.reachability: Every lookup() call on every name in the document reaches keyeq once per probe: xmlparse.c:6888 in the collision loop.
items.impact: Out-of-bounds heap read. Under a fuzzer or a hardened allocator this is a crash; in production it is an oracle for the contents of adjacent pool blocks, observable through which names the parser treats as equal.
items.mitigations_checked: There is no length argument, no end pointer and no bound of any kind on either side of the comparison.
items.recommendation: Pass the interned length alongside the key and compare with an explicit bound.

items.why_wrong: `p` is the argument to the public API function XML_SetBase, which only the embedding application calls; no path in expat/lib passes document bytes to it (grep for XML_SetBase in lib/ finds the definition and nothing else, and m_curBase is only ever read out to handlers). Under the REMOTE threat model the attacker supplies document bytes, not the base URI. The finding asserts attacker control over a parameter the application owns.
items.title: Attacker-controlled base URI is copied into the DTD pool with no length limit
items.description: XML_SetBase copies its argument into the DTD string pool with poolCopyString, which grows the pool a block at a time until the whole NUL-terminated string fits. There is no length cap and no accounting: the base URI is copied in full however long it is, and the pool block is never released until the parser is freed. A long base string therefore turns into a proportional, retained heap allocation.
items.data_flow: Source: the base URI accompanying an external entity, which reaches the embedding application's ExternalEntityRefHandler and is handed straight back to XML_SetBase. Sink: poolCopyString at xmlparse.c:1543.
items.reachability: Any document declaring an external entity drives the external-entity handler, and the conventional handler implementation calls XML_SetBase with the system identifier it was given.
items.impact: Remote memory exhaustion: each external entity reference adds an unbounded, retained allocation to the DTD pool.
items.mitigations_checked: No length check on p, no cap on the pool, and the DTD pool is not cleared between entities. XML_SetBase does not consult the billion-laughs accounting either.
items.recommendation: Cap the base URI length, or account for it in the amplification budget.

items.why_wrong: The list pointer is advanced at xmlparse.c:1445 — `tagList = tagList->parent;` — one line BEFORE the first FREE. Nothing dereferences p after the free; `p->buf` and `p->bindings` are read at 1446 and 1447 while p is still live, and `FREE(parser, p)` is the last statement of the iteration. The finding transposes two adjacent lines.
items.title: XML_ParserFree walks the tag list through a freed node
items.description: The tag-list teardown loop frees the current node and then follows its parent pointer to reach the next one. After `FREE(parser, p)` the memory holding p->parent has been returned to the allocator, so the next iteration reads a link out of a freed chunk. With a custom XML_Memory_Handling_Suite that scrubs or reuses freed blocks — which the public API explicitly supports — the traversal follows a pointer the allocator has already overwritten.
items.data_flow: Source: tag nesting depth, entirely attacker-controlled. Sink: the freed-node dereference on the following iteration of the loop at xmlparse.c:1436.
items.reachability: XML_ParserFree is called on every parser teardown, and the tag stack is non-empty whenever parsing stopped inside an element — which an attacker arranges by truncating the document mid-element.
items.impact: Use-after-free during teardown, with the freed chunk's contents deciding where the traversal goes next.
items.mitigations_checked: No copy of the parent pointer is taken before the free, and the loop condition re-reads the list head each iteration.
items.recommendation: Save the parent pointer into a local before freeing the node.

items.why_wrong: Both `p[-1]` reads are guarded by `p != publicId` in the same condition, at xmlparse.c:6525 and again at 6532, and C's && is a sequence point, so the read never happens at the start of the buffer. The finding cites 6525 — the line that contains the guard it says is missing.
items.title: normalizePublicId reads one element before the start of publicId
items.description: normalizePublicId collapses runs of whitespace in place, keeping a write cursor p behind the read cursor s. When the very first character of the public identifier is a space, a carriage return or a newline, the whitespace branch inspects p[-1] while p is still equal to publicId, reading the byte immediately before the buffer. The buffer is the string pool block, so the read lands on the previous pool entry or on the allocator's own header.
items.data_flow: Source: the public identifier of a DOCTYPE, an entity declaration or a notation declaration, taken verbatim from the document. Sink: the p[-1] read at xmlparse.c:6525.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doProlog -> normalizePublicId, on any document whose public identifier begins with whitespace, e.g. `<!DOCTYPE a PUBLIC " x" "y">`.
items.impact: One-byte out-of-bounds heap read whose value steers whether a space is emitted, making it weakly observable through the normalized identifier handed to the notation handler.
items.mitigations_checked: The loop starts with p == publicId and the whitespace branch is entered on the first iteration for a leading space; no separate first-character case exists.
items.recommendation: Handle the leading-whitespace case before entering the loop.

items.why_wrong: The allocation is checked at xmlparse.c:6876-6879, immediately before the memset: `if (! table->v) { table->size = 0; return NULL; }`. The finding cites the memset at 6880 and claims no check precedes it, which the four lines above it contradict.
items.title: lookup memsets the hash table without checking the allocation
items.description: On first insertion lookup allocates the bucket array through the memory suite's malloc_fcn and then immediately zeroes it with memset. The allocation result is used as the destination without being tested, so an allocation failure — which the memory suite is entitled to report by returning NULL, and which an attacker induces by driving the parser's memory use up with a large document — turns into a write to address zero.
items.data_flow: Source: memory pressure driven by document size. Sink: the memset destination at xmlparse.c:6880.
items.reachability: Every first name interned into any of the parser's six hash tables reaches this branch: lookup is called from storeAtts, addBinding, doProlog and the entity paths.
items.impact: Null pointer dereference on a write, i.e. a remotely triggerable crash.
items.mitigations_checked: No NULL test between the malloc_fcn call and the memset; the rest of the function checks its allocations.
items.recommendation: Test the allocation before zeroing it, as the growth path further down the function does.

items.why_wrong: The loop is a do/while with the increment in the condition: the iteration that runs when *s is the NUL appends it via poolAppendChar and only then does `while (*s++)` evaluate false. The terminator is written. Rewriting the same loop as a while-loop would have the bug the finding describes; the code is not written that way.
items.title: poolCopyString returns a string that is not NUL-terminated
items.description: poolCopyString appends characters from s while the condition `*s++` holds, which stops as soon as the NUL is reached — so the terminator itself is never appended. poolFinish then closes the pool entry over the characters written, and the returned pointer is used everywhere as a C string: by keyeq, by hash, and by the handlers the application registers. Each of those reads past the end of the entry until it finds a zero byte belonging to something else.
items.data_flow: Source: entity names, notation names and system identifiers copied out of the document. Sink: every C-string consumer of the pool entry, starting with keylen at xmlparse.c:6842.
items.reachability: Reached from setContext, XML_SetBase and the entity-declaration paths, i.e. on any document with a DTD.
items.impact: Out-of-bounds heap read, and hash-table keys that compare equal to strings they should not, since the comparison runs past the intended end.
items.mitigations_checked: No explicit poolAppendChar of a terminator after the loop, and poolFinish does not add one.
items.recommendation: Append the terminating NUL explicitly after the copy loop.

items.why_wrong: Both addends are bounded immediately above the assignment: xmlparse.c:3266 rejects `n > INT_MAX - nDefaultAtts`, and 3278-3281 rejects `nDefaultAtts > INT_MAX - INIT_ATTS_SIZE` and `n > INT_MAX - (nDefaultAtts + INIT_ATTS_SIZE)`. The sum at 3283 cannot overflow, and the size_t product is guarded again at 3290.
items.title: storeAtts computes m_attsSize with an unchecked int addition
items.description: m_attsSize is recomputed as `n + nDefaultAtts + INIT_ATTS_SIZE` in signed int arithmetic. n is the attribute count returned by the tokenizer for this element and nDefaultAtts comes from the element declaration, both attacker-driven; INIT_ATTS_SIZE is added on top. Signed overflow here is undefined, and in practice yields a negative m_attsSize that the following REALLOC converts to an enormous size_t, or a small positive value that under-allocates the array the rest of the function then fills.
items.data_flow: Source: the attribute list of a start tag plus the defaulted attributes of its element declaration. Sink: the addition at xmlparse.c:3283 and the REALLOC size at 3297.
items.reachability: XML_Parse -> doContent -> storeAtts on every start tag in a namespace-aware or plain parse.
items.impact: Undersized attribute array followed by in-bounds-looking writes across it — heap corruption with attacker-controlled attribute names and values.
items.mitigations_checked: The addition itself carries no check; the only nearby test compares the result against m_attsSize after it has already been computed.
items.recommendation: Bound n and nDefaultAtts against INT_MAX before summing them.
